headline: Phil Schiller steps down as Apple's App Store chief after 9 years
summary: Longtime Apple executive Phil Schiller is stepping down from his role leading the App Store. He will transition to an Apple Fellow position.
details: Phil Schiller, a key figure at Apple since 1987, has stepped down from his leadership of the App Store, a role he held since 2015. He is moving into an Apple Fellow position, a role typically reserved for employees with significant contributions to the company.

While Schiller will no longer manage the App Store's day-to-day operations, he will continue with Apple on unspecified projects. Insiders suggest this role may be a step towards his eventual retirement.

Schiller's tenure included overseeing the App Store during a significant antitrust lawsuit filed by Epic Games. While Apple largely won the case, it was ordered to allow developers to link to external payment options.

Carson Oliver, an Apple employee of over 14 years, will take over the daily operations of the App Store. The division is also being moved from the marketing department to the services division, led by Eddy Cue.

Schiller's departure follows a string of high-profile exits from Apple, including COO Jeff Williams, VP Lisa Jackson, General Counsel Kate Adams, and Apple Pay head Jennifer Bailey. Paul Meade, VP in charge of Vision Pro, also recently left for OpenAI.

headline_marked: Software engineers' new job: [[designing AI agent boundaries]]
headline: Software engineers' new job: designing AI agent boundaries
summary: As AI agents write more code, human roles are shifting from writing logic to abstract system design and governance.
details: The rise of AI coding assistants like Cursor and Claude Code has dramatically reduced the effort required to generate initial code implementations. Engineers can now describe complex tasks in plain English and have agents produce credible starting points, shifting the bottleneck away from writing syntax.

This evolution raises questions about the future role of software engineers. If AI agents become the primary authors of local system logic, the engineer's focus may transition from constructing code to a more abstract role, potentially involving reviewing and approving AI-generated pull requests.

Drawing parallels to thermodynamics, AI agents are computational engines that require direction to perform useful work. Prompts, requirements, or failing tests provide this intent, guiding the agent to generate code, tool calls, and system changes.

However, AI agents can accumulate 'operational entropy' by following stale assumptions or addressing symptoms rather than root causes. Without clear signals like failing tests, precise data contracts, or explicit feedback, agents can drift from correct outcomes.

Enterprise systems, unlike simpler coding tasks, rarely offer the stillness needed for AI convergence. Real-time engines, data platforms, and evolving APIs introduce complexity and mutable state, making AI-driven development challenging.

The 'three-body problem' from physics serves as a useful analogy for the complexity of modern enterprise software. Just as adding a third celestial body makes orbital prediction chaotic, the interplay of dynamic data, evolving code, and external dependencies makes AI-driven development unpredictable.
